description.sr_latin: Kako da zvučiš kao da si odrastao u Srbiji — ili bar da nasmešiš ekipu.
description.en: How to sound like you grew up in Serbia — or at least make the crew laugh.

phrases.context: Kicking off a juicy story or piece of gossip to a friend.
phrases.notes: 'Brate' is vocative of 'brat' (brother). Used constantly regardless of actual relation. Women use it too.

phrases.sr_latin: Brate moj, šta da ti kažem.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Брате мој, шта да ти кажем.
phrases.en: My brother, what can I tell you.
phrases.context: Exasperated resignation. When life is being life and there are no solutions.
Sympathetic but resigned. When someone tells you their problems and you feel for them but can't help.
phrases.notes: The 'e' at the start adds a wistful, philosophical tone.

phrases.context: Affectionate greeting or exclamation between close friends.
phrases.notes: Very warm and folksy. Has a Bosnian flavor — your best friend will appreciate this one.

phrases.context: Your buddy makes a ridiculous claim — playfully shoo him off with one sharp word.
phrases.notes: Short, sharp, iconic. One of the first words every Serbian kid learns.

phrases.context: Dismissal with a smile. 'Bre' is the quintessential Serbian particle — it softens or intensifies everything.
phrases.notes: 'Bre' has no direct translation. It's pure Serbian flavor. Add it to anything for authenticity.

phrases.context: Affectionate ribbing among friends. Tone makes it loving, not hurtful.
phrases.notes: 'Budala' is grammatically feminine even when referring to a man.

phrases.en: Don't be annoying. / Stop being a pain.
phrases.context: Your friend keeps nagging you about the same thing — tell him to quit being a pain.

phrases.en: Where you at, man? / What's up?
phrases.context: Street-casual greeting between friends — the dropped-consonant, extra-relaxed version of 'where you at'.
phrases.notes: The 'g' gets dropped in casual speech. Very natural, very street.

phrases.context: Informal hello to a friend, dressed up with the all-purpose Serbian particle for extra flavor.
Dismissing a topic. Can be comforting ('don't worry about it') or dismissive ('it's not worth discussing').
A friend apologizes for forgetting to call back — brush it off, it's fine.
phrases.notes: Literally 'there's no connection.' The Serbian attitude toward problems in two words.

phrases.context: Something is hilarious. Serbians exaggerate emotions as a lifestyle.
phrases.notes: 'Umreću od...' works with anything: 'gladi' (hunger), 'dosade' (boredom), 'vrućine' (heat).

phrases.en: I'm done. / I'm spent. / I cracked.
phrases.context: Exhaustion, laughter, or being overwhelmed. Literally 'I burst.'
phrases.notes: Female speaker: 'Pukla sam.' Extremely versatile slang.

phrases.en: This is madness. / This is a madhouse.
phrases.context: You're stuck in chaotic gridlocked traffic — sum up the scene in one exasperated line.
When you do something stupid and own it. Self-roasting is a Serbian art form.
When you mess up in a way that's completely on-brand for you.
After doing something cringeworthy. Delivered with a resigned sigh.
phrases.notes: Female speaker: 'Opet sam se obrukala.' 'Obrukati se' = to make a fool of yourself.

phrases.context: Theatrical self-pity. Delivered with maximum drama over minimum inconvenience.
When the universe is conspiring against you personally. Usually about trivial things.

phrases.en: What kind of life is this, bro.
phrases.context: Philosophical despair meets dark humor. The Serbian national mood in one sentence.
phrases.notes: Can be genuinely bleak or hilariously overdramatic. Usually the latter.

phrases.context: Dramatic declaration over minor setbacks — missed bus, phone battery at 5%, forgot wallet.
phrases.notes: Female: 'Propala sam.' Literally 'I have fallen through/perished.'

phrases.sr_latin: Smešno mi je što je tužno.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Смешно ми је што је тужно.
phrases.context: The core of Serbian humor — dark comedy about real life. Use after any depressing-but-relatable observation.
Ironic rallying cry before doing something stupid, unnecessary, or both.
When you have an opinion but sharing it would cause problems. Everyone knows you have thoughts.
phrases.notes: 'Ćutati' = to be silent. Saying this is the opposite of being silent, which is the joke.

phrases.context: A plan keeps falling apart and you're done with it — tell your friend to drop the whole thing.
phrases.notes: 'Terati' = to drive/push. There's a much more vulgar version everyone actually uses.

phrases.context: A friend asks how things are going — answer in one laid-back word that it's all relaxed.
phrases.notes: Literally 'lightly.' The Serbian equivalent of 'easy-peasy' or 'no worries.'

phrases.context: Telling someone to slow down and relax. Very Balkan philosophy — life is not a race.
phrases.notes: 'Polako' = slowly/easy. Core Balkan concept: rushing is suspicious.

phrases.context: Your friend is panicking about a small problem — reassure him there's nothing to stress about.
phrases.notes: 'Frka' = panic/stress. Very common among younger speakers.

phrases.context: You stub your toe on the table leg — let out the natural little cry.
phrases.notes: The Swiss Army knife of Serbian exclamations. You'll hear it dozens of times a day.

phrases.context: Encouragement, impatience, agreement, farewell — depends on context. Possibly the most versatile Serbian word.
phrases.notes: As goodbye: 'Ajde, ćao!' As encouragement: 'Ajde, možeš ti to!' As impatience: 'Ajde, požuri!'

phrases.context: A friend asks if you were upset about it — wave it off with a laid-back no.
phrases.notes: 'Jok' comes from Turkish. Short, punchy, very natural sounding.

phrases.context: Getting someone's attention before sharing news, gossip, or a joke.

phrases.en: That's pure spite. / That's stubbornness out of principle.
phrases.context: Someone keeps doing the thing they were told not to, just to prove a point — name it for what it is.
phrases.notes: 'Inat' is an untranslatable concept — stubborn defiance, doing something specifically because someone told you not to. National trait.

phrases.context: A friend suggests something you think is a waste of time — dismiss it as lame.
phrases.notes: Literally 'without connection.' Opposite of good. Very commonly used dismissal.

phrases.context: Your friend finally lands on the exact song you wanted — light up and confirm it.
phrases.notes: Also used to wrap up a conversation or declare something finished.

phrases.context: Your friend is hesitating before a bold move — egg him on to go all in.
phrases.notes: Literally 'only strong.' The Serbian version of 'YOLO' but with more conviction.
